Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Analyst (New Grad, 2027) role. I'm a senior at Brookfield University and will finish a B.S. in Computer Science with a minor in Data Science in May 2027. The role combines SQL and dashboards with survey and interview data for education, healthcare and nonprofit clients. That's very close to the work I've done in an analytics internship and in an HCI research lab.

This past summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. For the product team, I built a Tableau dashboard of weekly student engagement covering active students, lessons completed and streaks, and I wrote the SQL behind it. While building it, I found that sessions were being counted twice when students sent the app to the background. I redefined a session as activity with gaps under 30 minutes, using LAG over event timestamps, so the weekly numbers matched real use. My manager found the breakdown of streaks by grade level especially useful.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I work on an interview study, led by a PhD student, about how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages and ran the eligibility screener. I also transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools and community names with placeholders, and coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. When the project lead and I checked how consistently we coded, we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of resolving disagreements. This work taught me to handle sensitive data about young people carefully and to make qualitative coding consistent. I would use both skills at Pinecrest when coding open-ended survey responses and helping with stakeholder interviews.

In a Machine Learning course project, my team of three fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I did the error analysis, which showed that the model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. It reminded me that a metric only means something once you look at the people behind the data.

What draws me to Pinecrest is your focus on helping organizations understand the students, patients and members they serve. I'd welcome the chance to learn from your senior researchers, work in two client domains during the first year, and practice turning analysis into clear recommendations for clients.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos
M2: At Khoury, I would be excited to work with Prof. Tianshi Li. Her PEACH Lab takes the position that problems raised by AI can't be solved by improving models alone and also need human-centered approaches that empower people. That idea is at the core of what I want to study. When a sentiment or moderation tool misreads a teen's dark humor as a crisis, or misses real distress, a better classifier is only part of the answer. The rest depends on how people work alongside these tools. Her group's work on human oversight of AI agents asks a related question in a different setting: when an automated system should hand control back to a person. I would like to explore that question in online support communities, where peer moderators already make these judgment calls. I am also drawn to the lab's mixed-methods approach, which combines interviews and user studies with building and evaluating models. That's the combination I want to train in, and it builds on both my qualitative work in the Social Computing Lab and my experience training and analyzing classifiers.

# Statement of Purpose
**Avery Santos**

I'm a senior at Brookfield University, majoring in Computer Science with a minor in Data Science. For the past year I've been a research assistant in the Social Computing Lab. That experience is the main reason I'm applying to PhD programs.

**What I've done so far**

In October 2025 I joined J. Kim's interview study in Prof. A. Moreno's lab. The study looks at how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. My role has been supporting the study, not leading it. I sent recruitment messages, ran the eligibility screener, transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, and coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. When J. Kim and I compared our coding on two transcripts, we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of talking through our disagreements. The paper is now under review.

I liked transcribing more than I expected, even though it's slow. Listening closely to the same conversation over and over, you notice things you'd miss the first time. I've also learned a lot from working with J. I've seen how a study is built and how carefully decisions get made. I haven't yet done those parts myself: choosing a question, designing a study and deciding what counts as an answer. They're what I want to learn.

**What I keep wondering about**

In a Machine Learning class, my team of three trained a model to classify sentiment in Reddit mental-health support posts. My part was the error analysis. A lot of the posts the model got wrong weren't negative in a simple way. People were joking about bad things, and the model couldn't tell.

Later, one interview I transcribed stayed with me. A participant described automated moderation removing posts in a community that mattered to them. I understand why moderators use tools like that. But I keep wondering who those tools are actually for, and how automated moderation changes what teens feel they can say when they're looking for help. I'm not sure yet, but it feels related to what I saw in my class project. In both cases, an automated system was reading people in a way that didn't match what they meant.

I don't think this is a full research question yet. It's the question I keep coming back to, and I'd like to learn how to turn it into one.

**Why Khoury**

I'm interested in Prof. Tianshi Li's PEACH Lab. Her lab works mostly on privacy and AI. What draws me is its view that problems with AI need human-centered work, not only better models. That matches what I took away from my class project. I'd also like to learn the lab's mix of methods, which includes interviews and user studies alongside building and testing models. [Add one sentence about something specific from her work, in your own words, after you've read it.]

**Why a PhD**

I could keep doing analysis work, and I'm applying to those jobs too. But a job wouldn't let me follow a question like this one. I want to learn how to take a project from a question to a finished study, with the kind of mentorship I've had from J. I'd bring care with sensitive data, experience with both qualitative coding and machine learning, and a real interest in why systems get people wrong.
